records.title: Night crossings on the Likoni channel
records.summary: A retired ferry deckhand recalls how crews managed crowding, life-jacket storage and passenger flow during the busiest evening crossings.
records.creator: Remembering the Waters field team

transcript.text: We used to count heads at the ramp. Not exactly, but enough to know when to stop people.
The life jackets were in the boxes under the benches. Many passengers never knew they were there.
So we started telling them. Every crossing, one sentence: the jackets are under your seat.
In the evenings the crowd pushed hard. The rope at the gate mattered more than any rule on paper.
What I want young people to know is this: the water does not care how late you are.
Wait for the next ferry. That is the whole lesson.

records.title: Boat registration and safety equipment checklist
records.summary: Sample scan of a typed checklist issued to boat owners, listing required equipment: bailer, paddles, a lamp and one buoyancy aid per crew member.
records.body:
SAFETY EQUIPMENT REQUIRED ON EVERY REGISTERED VESSEL
1. One approved buoyancy aid for each person on board.
2. A bailer secured to the hull.
3. Two paddles, whether or not an engine is fitted.
4. A lamp or torch for travel after sunset.
5. The registration number painted clearly on both sides.
Vessels found without the above may be detained until equipment is fitted.
records.creator: Fisheries office (sample)

records.title: The afternoon wind on Lake Turkana
records.summary: A fisherwoman from Kalokol describes reading the sudden afternoon winds and the community rule of returning to shore before they rise.
records.body: My grandmother taught us to watch the hills to the east. When the dust lifts there, the wind will reach the water before you can finish mending a net. We had a rule: when the sun passes the top of the sky, the boats turn home. Nobody wrote it down, but everybody knew it. Some of the young men who came from outside did not know, and that is when people were lost. Now we tell every newcomer on the first day.
records.creator: Remembering the Waters field team

records.title: Rescue swimmers of Lamu
records.summary: Sample video interview with a member of a volunteer rescue group describing how dhow crews organised informal search and rescue.
records.creator: Remembering the Waters field team

transcript.text: When a boat was late, the whole jetty knew within minutes.
We did not have radios at first. We had the strongest swimmers and the fastest dhow.
Later we learned to keep a list: who left, when, and where they were going.
That list saved more lives than any of us swimming.
Today every boat should tell someone on shore. It costs nothing.

records.title: Lake Naivasha boating incident summary (sample)
records.summary: Sample typed incident summary describing a capsized tourist boat, the causes identified and recommendations for life-jacket use by visitors.
records.body:
INCIDENT SUMMARY - FOR COMMITTEE USE
A small boat carrying visitors capsized in rough water during the late afternoon.
All passengers were recovered by nearby boats. Two required hospital care.
Findings: life jackets were on board but not worn; boat exceeded its seating capacity.
Recommendation: operators to ensure every visitor wears a life jacket before departure.
Recommendation: a visible capacity plate to be fixed on every hire boat.
records.creator: Local safety committee (sample)

records.title: Crossing the Tana River in flood season
records.summary: A farmer from Garsen recounts canoe crossings during the long rains, and how villages agreed on safe crossing points.
records.creator: Remembering the Waters field team

transcript.text: In the long rains the river becomes another animal.
We chose one crossing place for everybody, where the bank was firm and the current slower.
Children never crossed alone. An elder always held the rope at the bow.
When the water was brown and fast, we waited. Even one day.
Patience was our life jacket.

records.title: Learning to swim at Shimoni
records.summary: A teacher describes starting free swimming lessons for children in a fishing village after a near-drowning on the reef flats.
records.body: Most of the children in our village live beside the sea, yet very few could swim. After one of my pupils was pulled from the water at low tide, we asked the fishermen to help us. On Saturday mornings they stood in the shallows while the children practised floating. In three years more than two hundred children learned. The fishermen say the lessons taught them something too: to wear the jackets they were asking the children to respect.
records.creator: Submitted by community member (sample)

records.title: Hippos, reeds and night fishing on Lake Baringo
records.summary: A fisherman explains how hippo movements shaped where and when canoes went out, and the signals used between boats at night.
records.creator: Remembering the Waters field team

transcript.text: The hippo is the master of this lake. We are only visitors.
At night we kept to the open water and away from the reeds where they rest.
Two knocks on the hull meant 'I am here'. Three knocks meant 'come quickly'.
Those knocks were older than any telephone.

records.title: Community beach safety notice, Usenge
records.summary: Sample transcription of a hand-painted notice board at a landing beach, setting out local rules agreed by the beach management unit.
records.body:
BEACH RULES - AGREED BY ALL MEMBERS
No boat leaves without telling the beach office its crew and destination.
Every crew member wears a jacket from the beach store.
No fishing when the warning flag is raised.
Boats return before the evening storm bell.
records.creator: Beach management unit (sample)

records.title: Malindi glass-bottom boat operators
records.summary: Draft testimony from a tour boat operator about briefing visitors on reef safety. Awaiting metadata review before publication.
records.body: Before any visitor steps on the boat we explain three things: where the jackets are, what to do if they fall in, and why they must not stand on the coral. The briefing takes two minutes. It used to feel like a delay. Now visitors thank us for it.
records.creator: Remembering the Waters field team
